item.title: As African space race heats up, Senegal pursues homemade satellites
item.description: Senegalese engineers in hairnets and white gloves are carefully assembling a nanosatellite at a French lab—another step toward fostering their own space industry back home. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reading app boosts kids' literacy
item.description: A new Flinders University study of primary school children shows a science-based digital phonics reading app can accelerate early reading while helping teachers quickly identify students needing extra support. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 66.5-million-year-old trackway captures adult T. rex at walking pace
item.description: Scientists from the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and Liverpool John Moores University in England have discovered the first adult T. rex trackway, providing insights into how this emblematic predator moved. The findings are published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anak Krakatau erupts, disrupting 300,000 travelers as 1883 disaster looms large
item.description: Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatau has erupted again this week, sending plumes of volcanic ash high into the sky and disrupting hundreds of flights. More than 300,000 passengers have been affected. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hidden microplastic pollution in Swiss waters uncovered
item.description: Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 millimeters that originate either from manufactured products or from the breakdown of larger plastic items. They can now be found everywhere, from oceans and rivers to soils and indoor air. Because most plastics degrade very slowly, these particles can remain in the environment for decades or centuries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US scrambles to match China’s air-breathing hypersonic missiles with Darpa programme
item.description: A year after China unveiled the world’s first operational air-breathing hypersonic missiles, the United States is launching a programme to double down on developing similar weapons. The US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (Darpa) will bring contractors together later this month to lay out what it wants from the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile, with air-breathing propulsion at the heart of the project, according to the agency’s website. Unlike rocket-powered missiles,... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: More than numbers: First global dataset shows who is immigrating
item.description: As countries compete for skilled workers and grapple with aging populations and labor shortages, understanding who is moving across borders is increasingly important. A new study provides the first global data set of immigration composition disaggregated simultaneously by age, sex and educational attainment, offering a new basis for tracking brain gain and brain drain and improving population projections. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient DNA reveals 1,000 years of human-environment interactions at Crawford Lake
item.description: An international team of scientists has recreated a 1,000-year timeline documenting ecological changes and human impact on the area surrounding Crawford Lake, the famed location of the proposed Anthropocene. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heat forces French Champagne makers to stiffen their drink
item.description: Drinking this year's champagne might cause a heftier headache as France's record heat waves force some producers to increase alcohol levels, industry officials said Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
item.description: An experimental compound called AP503 significantly strengthened bones in mice by activating GPR133, a receptor that boosts bone formation while slowing bone loss. Because the same treatment has also been linked to stronger muscles, researchers see intriguing potential for combating age-related decline and osteoporosis. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ancient bones reveal that cannibalism took different forms in Neolithic Spain
item.description: Cannibalism was sometimes on the Neolithic menu, as numerous archaeological discoveries have revealed. But while ancient human bones show the practice took place, far less evidence exists about the forms it may have taken or why people occasionally consumed one another. Was it to stave off hunger during times of desperation? Did different tribes eat their defeated enemies? Or was cannibalism part of complex rituals? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In North Carolina, a race is on to restore critical peatland before it dries up or is destroyed
item.description: The birds are up with the sunrise—warblers, flycatchers, sparrows and towhees calling across the treetops. Deer browse on tender buds emerging from dense shrubs. Black bears scrounge for roots, insects and other edibles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could quantum protocols make electronic voting more secure?
item.description: Electronic voting, the use of electronic systems to cast, record or count votes, could potentially simplify the process of electing new political leaders or other representatives. While some countries have already started using internet-connected devices or electronic voting machines at polling stations, the trustworthiness, security and anonymity of electronic voting systems are still widely debated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy of organic molecules in organic solvents for applying organic reactions
item.description: In research published in the journal Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, the electronic structures of organic molecules containing sp2-hybridized carbons in organic solvents were studied using C K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), termed "Soft-XAS-OS." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI ‘Could Kill Us All,’ Warns Anthropic Researcher as He Quits the Company: AI Companies Are ‘Gambling With Our Lives’
item.description: Multiple current and former Anthropic employees warned — and admitted — on Tuesday that the researchers building new AI models believe the technology could lead to humanity’s destruction by the end of the decade, reflecting the industry’s frenzy over reining in rapid development. Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, wrote on X that he […] Fuente: Variety.
item.dc:creator: Corbin Bolies

item.title: NASA Names Two Artemis II Astronauts to Emeritus Program
item.description: Following their landmark Artemis II mission earlier this year, distinguished NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning in September to emeritus status at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. In an emeritus role, individuals with a high degree of technical and professional knowledge can continue to support the agency by donating their […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gerelle Q. Dodson

item.title: Study into career shocks finds what doesn't break expats makes them stronger
item.description: New research challenges the idea that career shocks are bad news for expatriate workers, finding that major personal, professional or societal disruptions can instead act as a catalyst for adaptation and resilience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biologists find a hidden weak spot in how bacteria build the tails they use to move
item.description: New research from Indiana University has uncovered a previously unknown vulnerability in how bacteria build the whip-like tails they use to move. The researchers found that building these tails can put stress on the protective wall surrounding a bacterial cell and uncovered systems bacteria use to keep that stress from becoming destructive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ozempic and Wegovy linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks
item.description: Semaglutide, the drug found in Ozempic and Wegovy, was linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks in a large real-world study. It was also associated with about 20% fewer COPD flare-ups. Researchers say GLP-1 drugs may offer respiratory benefits in addition to their effects on diabetes and obesity, but clinical trials are needed to confirm the findings. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Pounding waves open up sinkhole in swanky Malibu
item.description: Pounding surf lashing the swanky California enclave of Malibu on Tuesday opened a giant sinkhole in the driveway of a house reportedly belonging to U.S. actor Nicolas Cage. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Local microbes persist in wine despite commercial yeast
item.description: A new study has demonstrated that regional microbial imprints can remain detectable under commercial winemaking conditions. The research, appearing in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, shows that inoculated fermentations do not "override" native microbial diversity and that vineyard management and environmental conditions affect wine quality. The study helps explain why wines from different regions taste distinct even when made with similar techniques and supports regional flavors and branding. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Taxing billionaires and redistributing wealth could save millions of lives amid global aid cuts
item.description: Wealth redistribution policies currently under discussion in international forums could avert between 6.6 million and 29.5 million deaths by 2030, according to a study published in The Lancet and led by ISGlobal in collaboration with other leading economic and health research institutions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Canada eyes researchers looking to leave 'hostile' US
item.description: Fed up with funding restrictions surrounding her research on links between climate change and health, American epidemiologist Sheryl Magzamen has left the United States for Canada. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can a messy person become a tidy person? Or are we doomed?
item.description: Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the closet, and their kitchen counter remains mysteriously visible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some police officers use the 'bad guys' label to provide moral clarity
item.description: A new study shows that some U.S. police officers often use the term "bad guys" to describe people who commit crimes, especially when faced with ambiguity in their work. It is a label officers may use to reduce complex and morally challenging situations and contexts into a clearer, more legible framework. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MTM's selfie footage of BepiColombo's eight-year journey
item.description: Video: 00:04:20 Witness how over the last eight years, the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has been travelling through the inner Solar System and aligning itself with Mercury's orbit. So far, it has travelled 9.9 billion km and completed nine 'planetary flybys' to help steer its way. In the video, you can see the spacecraft fly past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times. Since launching on 20 October 2018, BepiColombo has been travelling as a composite spacecraft made up of ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), and the Mercury Transfer… Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: How companies quietly undercut dissent
item.description: In 2016, when Amazon workers began organizing at a warehouse in Chester, Virginia, the company tracked where employees gathered, posted anti-union messaging in bathroom stalls and held town halls to discourage them. The National Labor Relations Board forced Amazon to admit, in writing, that it had illegally surveilled and threatened workers. The union drive still failed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A wandering black hole caught feeding on the run
item.description: Astronomers have found the first direct evidence that a wandering black hole can feed itself by dragging gas along in its wake as it moves through its galaxy. It's the first direct evidence of an accretion channel long predicted in theory but never before observed. The paper describing this discovery was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 11. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers discuss how data center construction could influence voters and impact public land
item.description: The construction of new data centers is shaping up to be a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections. Politicians in both parties have been distancing themselves from data centers in the face of public discontent around the issue, with public backlash leading to the freezing of dozens of data center projects nationwide this year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
item.description: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Q&A: What can rent prices reveal about inflation and the economy?
item.description: Tracking rent prices may help businesses and policymakers understand where inflation is headed months in advance of government inflation reports, according to researchers at Penn State's Smeal College of Business who developed the Penn State/ACY Alternative Inflation Index. The Penn State index was recently incorporated into the Bloomberg Terminal, a software system that serves financial professionals with real-time market data, news and analytics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Alaska saw 30,000 ship arrivals in 11 years; their hulls created a hidden invasive species risk
item.description: Researchers found that nearly 30,000 commercial vessel arrivals brought 430 sq km of submerged surface area to Alaska between 2012 and 2022. The study says this surface can carry marine organisms through biofouling. Passenger vessels accounted for more than half of the total area, while warming waters and increased Arctic shipping could raise the risk of non-indigenous species reaching Alaska. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: OpenAI says 10,000 AI agents cracked one of math's hardest problems in 88 hours
item.description: OpenAI said Tuesday that one of its unreleased artificial intelligence models had solved a mathematical puzzle that has eluded mathematicians for generations, a claim that also drew a fight with rival researchers over credit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Meet Franklin Howley-Dumit Serulle, whose online insect photo helped reveal a new hoverfly
item.description: An amateur naturalist's photograph on iNaturalist helped scientists identify a new hoverfly species. Researchers later found a specimen in Valle Nuevo National Park, confirming the discovery. This new species, Monoceromyia ndidiae, was formally described after laboratory analysis. The discovery highlights how amateur observations contribute to understanding biodiversity. This finding earned the Swiss Systematics Society’s New Species of the Year 2026 title. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Tylenol use in pregnancy linked to reproductive changes in baby girls, study finds
item.description: Smaller ovarian and uterine volume and fewer ovarian follicles seen in babies exposed to Tylenol in womb Fuente: The Independent - World.

item.title: ¿Y si el calor que desprende tu coche se pudiera convertir en frío para tu casa en verano? Estos científicos han encontrado una manera de hacerlo (y sin electricidad)
item.description: Usar el calor que sobra para producir frío. Aunque parezca magia, hoy estamos un paso más cerca de hacerlo realidad. Los investigadores del Instituto Tecnológico de Karlsruhe en Alemania y de la Universidad de Tsukuba en Japón han conseguido desarrollar un prototipo que convierte las altas temperaturas en aire fresco. Y para colmo, lo hace sin necesidad de un motor eléctrico. No es brujería. Es tecnología elastocalórica. Este dispositivo usa dos películas ultrafinas de níquel y titanio que tienen memoria de forma, cada una con una función diferente. En un primer paso, cuando se expone a una… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Ramírez

item.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is bursting with methanol
item.description: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains exceptionally high levels of methanol, suggesting it formed under conditions very different from those that shaped most comets in our solar system. ALMA also revealed that tiny icy grains around the comet are releasing methanol like miniature comets, giving astronomers an unusually detailed look at an object from another star system. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Families' interest in their kids' education is falling around the globe as scores drop, test shows
item.description: Families' interest in their kids' education is falling in many high-income countries as school systems struggle with plunging test scores, according to newly released results from a standardized test taken by 15-year-olds around the world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: These bulbs have evolved to avoid being eaten. You can take advantage of that
item.description: There's little worse in a gardener's mind than watching their careful planning and hard work go up in a cloud of teeth, thanks to every four-legged freeloader within chewing distance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI D-Day weather forecast falters under pressure
item.description: Today's best weather computers would still have struggled to accurately predict the weather for the D-Day landings, University of Reading research shows. The new research, published in the journal Weather ahead of the release of the D-Day film "Pressure," used AI models to produce 50 different forecasts of the storm that famously pushed back the Allies' invasion of Normandy in June 1944. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US firm used AI to hijack WeChat account, spurring call for cyber cooperation with China
item.description: US cybersecurity researchers have demonstrated how artificial intelligence could help hijack WeChat accounts via unanswered voice calls, intensifying concerns about AI-driven cyber threats and prompting renewed calls for bilateral cooperation between the United States and China. US security firm Calif said on Tuesday that its AI system identified a critical flaw in Tencent Holdings’ widely used messaging and payments app in July. In just a little over a week, researchers developed WeWorm – an... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Xinmei Shen

item.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
item.description: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Calculative mindsets linked to greater willingness to bend moral rules
item.description: In new research in the PsyCh Journal, people who tended to analyze experiences as mathematical cost-benefit problems were more likely to ignore moral rules. This tendency was associated with a greater willingness to make ethical compromises for money or status, as well as to accept immoral help when it benefited them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Daily Quiz | On Sir John Herschel’s contributions to early photography
item.description: On September 9, 1839, Sir John Herschel made what is regarded as the earliest surviving photograph on glass and made important contributions to astronomy and photography Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
item.description: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 4995-5001: 5,000 (Martian) Days on Mars
item.description: Written by William Farrand, Senior Research Scientist, Space Science Institute Earth planning date: Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 The span of sols spanned by this blog post is noteworthy in several ways. First, Curiosity became a world-class (for Mars at least) mountaineer by passing the 1 kilometer mark of elevation from its landing site on the floor […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: MTG-I2 reaches its final orbit
item.description: Europe’s Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2) satellite has reached its designated orbit at 36 000 km from Earth and is ready to begin its commissioning phase, preparing it to provide years of service to improve weather forecasting over Europe and North Africa. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Chinese scientists find a hidden atomic structure that unlocks methane
item.description: Scientists found that a tiny atomic structure that forms on nickel oxide during methane conversion is more effective than the metallic nickel long believed to drive the reaction. The discovery allowed a low-nickel catalyst to rival one containing 10 times more metal, potentially opening the door to cheaper and more efficient industrial catalysts. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 240-million-year-old lost fossil revealed a new reptile related to dinosaurs and crocodiles
item.description: The discovery of Silescelida acristata, a fossil unearthed in Brazil, provides crucial insights into the origins of early archosauriform reptiles. This remarkable creature thrived at a pivotal time, just before the dawn of dinosaurs. While only partial remains were found, its distinctive bone structures set it apart from contemporaneous Triassic reptiles. Phylogenetic studies classify Silescelida as an early variant of eucrocopodan archosauriforms. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Europeans want a united Europe but question whether it can get there, study finds
item.description: A continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline, report suggests Europeans overwhelmingly want a strong, united and independent Europe but question whether it can get there, according to a study that suggests a continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline. The report , based on 5,800 interviews in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and the UK and analysis of the way Europe is discussed in the politics and media of 15 countries, paints a picture of an ambitious but… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Jon Henley Europe correspondent

item.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
item.description: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Anak Krakatau Rumbles Again
item.description: A powerful eruption from the Indonesian volcano lofted ash into the atmosphere, disrupting thousands of flights and degrading air quality. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
item.description: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study. Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Kat Lay, Global health correspondent

item.title: GPS collars reveal secrets of the power struggle between lions and hyenas in the wild
item.description: Hidden deep in the bush, ranging over huge territories at speeds humans can't match and through terrain not even the most rugged vehicle can handle, hyenas and lions are hard to study. Now, new research using GPS collars to map the movements of individual animals has revealed crucial information about the relationship between these competing carnivore species. We've long assumed that hyenas simply shadow lions for scraps, but these findings show that when they encounter each other, it's the lions, especially males, that approach hyenas, and the hyenas that give way. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dark energy debunked? Cosmic acceleration may be an illusion
item.description: A new analysis of more than 1,700 supernovae is questioning whether the universe is really accelerating at all. After accounting for the ages of the stars that produce these explosions, researchers found signs that cosmic expansion may actually be slowing. They also argue that the apparent acceleration changes with direction, which would be difficult to explain with dark energy. Other cosmologists dispute the conclusion, setting up a major test for upcoming observatories. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Roman cemetery dig reveals Stone Age man buried with 2 skulls, 42 teeth and an axe
item.description: In a startling archaeological find, researchers uncovered a burial site dating back to the Stone Age, predating nearby Roman graves by thousands of years. The grave contained a battle axe, striking amber beads, and a unique necklace fashioned from the teeth of 42 animals. Additionally, two human skulls were discovered alongside the skeleton, offering rare insights into the rituals and practices of ancient communities. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Astronomers detect ancient hydrogen signal that could help map the Universe
item.description: Astronomers have detected an exceptionally faint hydrogen radio signal from billions of light-years away using South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope. Instead of finding galaxies one at a time, the technique measures their combined hydrogen glow across enormous stretches of space. The successful detection shows that astronomers may soon be able to create much larger 3D maps of the Universe. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Grooming-related messages reach almost two-thirds of children
item.description: Nearly two-thirds of Australian children surveyed in a recent study received at least one form of grooming-related communication from a stranger online in the past year, while almost one-third reported receiving direct requests for sexual information or interactions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chesapeake Bay underwater grasses increase 7%, buoyed by gains in salty waters
item.description: Submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV), one of the Chesapeake Bay's most important indicators of ecosystem health, increased by 7% in 2025, according to researchers at William & Mary's VIMS & Batten School. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A vicarious calibration model enables quantitative applications of Fengyun-3 satellite ocean color data
item.description: Ocean color remote sensing is a vital tool for monitoring global ocean carbon sinks and primary productivity. However, the on-orbit calibration accuracy of satellite sensors is insufficient, and weak marine signals account for only approximately 10% of the signals received by satellites, leading to significant uncertainties in ocean color remote-sensing applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why does Southeast Asia keeps breathing the same haze—and can ASEAN do more to stop it?
item.description: Southeast Asia has spent decades trying to tackle haze from forest fires. Yet every few years, the region finds itself breathing it again. The transboundary environmental problem has become a recurrent phenomenon in the region. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New computational method pushes cryo-electron microscopy beyond traditional resolution limits
item.description: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has become a powerful tool for determining the structures of proteins, viruses and molecular complexes at near-atomic resolution. However, achievable resolution is fundamentally limited by the Nyquist sampling frequency, which is determined by detector pixel size and microscope magnification. Once this physical limit is reached, researchers typically must recollect data at higher magnification, requiring additional microscope time, increased storage capacity and often fewer particles per image. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny backpacks reveal the secret, sometimes circuitous migrations of small songbirds
item.description: Squinting through my binoculars, I scanned the dense branches of a black spruce, trying my best to catch a glimpse of the thin legs of a small black, white and yellow songbird. I was on the hunt for a yellow-rumped warbler—a bird affectionately called "butter-butt" by birdwatchers after the distinctive buttery yellow patch of feathers above its tail. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some black holes grow much faster than their galaxies
item.description: Nearly every galaxy has a supermassive black hole. The few that don't have had theirs ejected during a galactic collision. That's because galaxies and their black holes have formed hand in hand. There is still some debate as to whether galaxies formed around the seeds of supermassive black holes or the other way around, but there is plenty of evidence to support the idea that the two evolve together. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Caffeine may flip an ancient cellular switch linked to slower aging
item.description: Scientists found that caffeine activates an ancient cellular energy system involved in stress resistance, DNA repair, and growth. The discovery could help explain caffeine’s links to healthier aging and may point toward new ways to target the same pathway. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: During some days in August, science takes center stage. The experts are surveying the little-known diversity of fungi found in the alpine Dryas heath. They may even discover species that have never been described scientifically before. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: One of the oldest known 3D fossils of an animal has been discovered in a sheep field in the Norwegian Arctic, the first new major site of its kind anywhere in Europe in decades. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Germany's 15-year-olds post lowest PISA results since testing began 25 years ago
item.description: The PISA study regularly assesses 15-year-olds' ability to understand and solve real-life problems in reading, mathematics and science toward the end of their compulsory education. It demonstrates the extent to which young people are prepared for the demands of a knowledge-based society and can participate in social life on their own terms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers rewire ribosomes to specialize in one protein
item.description: Every cell relies on ribosomes, the molecular machines that read genetic instructions and use them to assemble proteins. A cell needs thousands of types of proteins at any one time, so ribosomes must be generalists, capable of using instructions to produce any protein. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny molecular rings open new ways for designing better medicines
item.description: Cyclopropanes are organic chemistry's smallest rings. Three carbon atoms are joined in a triangle, creating a compact and unusually strained structure. Despite—or partly because of—this unusual geometry, cyclopropanes are found in many biologically active natural products and have important applications in medicines and drug discovery, from antidepressants to antibiotics and antiviral research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Prehistoric builders hauled 25-tonne stones at least 18 km to build iconic Devil's Arrows
item.description: New research has revealed that ancient builders deliberately transported enormous 25-tonne stones across at least 18 kilometers (11 miles) to build Britain's tallest surviving prehistoric stone row—the iconic Devil's Arrows. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Untangling the meta-biomaterial puzzle one property at a time
item.description: From repairing damaged tissues to developing better implants, many medical developments depend on materials that can mimic the complex properties of human tissue. Meta-biomaterials are among the most promising candidates. By tailoring their geometry, researchers can create materials with properties similar to those of natural tissues. But there is a catch: Changing one property often changes several others at the same time. TU Delft scientists have now developed a method to decouple these properties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new mission could rendezvous with Halley's Comet in 2061
item.description: Halley's Comet captures the imagination in a way that few other astronomical objects do. When it last made its approach toward the sun (admittedly when this author, who is now middle-aged, was 1 year old in 1986), humanity responded with a fleet of spacecraft known informally as the "Halley Armada." Yet because of the comet's trajectory, those spacecraft were only able to visit their target for a fleeting few hours, leaving planetary scientists wanting more. Now, a new paper by researchers at Khalifa University and their co-authors, available on the arXiv preprint server, describes a mission… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Grandchildren repay childhood care by supporting ailing grandparents in Hong Kong
item.description: As Hong Kong Special Administrative Region's population ages at one of the fastest rates in the world, demand for family elder care increases daily. To understand the responsibilities and roles assumed by grandchildren in caring for their grandparents, the Asia-Pacific Institute of Aging Studies (APIAS) at Lingnan University conducted an in-depth interview study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sparse-data method estimates sea surface temperatures 40% more accurately than conventional approach
item.description: Researchers have developed a method for extrapolating sea surface temperatures from sparse data that is significantly more accurate than other commonly used computational methods and slightly more accurate than the best-performing AI model, while taking a fraction of the time to train. The work has implications for both short-term weather forecasting and longer-term climate predictions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why does microwaving fish smell so bad?
item.description: The work break room can be a place of rest, gossip, fun or recovery. But it can also be a cause for complaint when yesterday's fish dinner becomes a smelly microwaved lunch. For most people, microwaving fish at work is a big no-no. It has even led to armed confrontations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Extremely massive galaxy proto-supercluster smashes distance record
item.description: An international team of astronomers has discovered the most distant progenitor to a galaxy supercluster ever. The discovery supports existing theories of how galaxy clusters evolve and reveals how they are connected to the larger cosmic web. The study relies largely on data from the ODIN survey, conducted with the U.S. Department of Energy-fabricated Dark Energy Camera on the U.S. National Science Foundation Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cosmic radiation at flight altitudes rises when the sun is less active
item.description: Radiation from space is constantly entering Earth's atmosphere, but how much of it reaches the altitudes used by commercial aircraft depends not only on height and location, but also on the activity of the sun. A new study based on high-altitude balloon measurements over southern Israel has mapped these changes through the atmosphere and found that radiation levels at aviation altitudes rise as solar activity falls. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Waterlogged seeds reveal melons' ancient journey
item.description: Melons produce many seeds, making the melon shape a traditional symbol of fertility and prosperity in Chinese culture. But the historical debate about how melons made their way to modern tables is as long and twisted as the vines they grow on. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA technique for manipulating satellite photos now reveals ancient images
item.description: High in the central tower of Angkor Wat, an ancient Cambodian temple, paintings depict horseback riders and a traditional musical ensemble. Thousands of visitors pass these images daily without noticing them because they are faded to the point of invisibility. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Helium-3 lifts new quantum computing concept with faster tunneling rates
item.description: Helium—the lightest atom that can be laser-cooled and controlled—powers a new design for high-powered, stable quantum computers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A crystalline sponge reveals structures of large 'beyond rule of 5' molecules
item.description: Drug discovery has traditionally followed the "rule of 5," which identifies chemical properties generally associated with good absorption of orally administered drugs, including a molecular weight below 500 daltons (Da). However, some pharmaceutical compounds fall outside these guidelines. Known as beyond rule of 5 (bRo5) molecules, these compounds can have larger, more complex structures while still exhibiting strong therapeutic activity and favorable pharmacological properties. Their size and structural complexity, however, make it difficult to characterize them using conventional methods… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: No evidence that Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs have improved child protection outcomes
item.description: New research concludes that Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs (MASHs) are failing to provide better protection for children in England, instead causing families distress and putting more pressure on social care resources. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Not all eggs are the same—uncovering a tropical parasite's secret weapons
item.description: A team of scientists from the Faculty of Science at Charles University has achieved a major breakthrough in research into schistosomiasis, a serious tropical disease affecting more than 250 million people worldwide. Using advanced laser microdissection, the researchers have, for the first time, captured and analyzed proteins secreted by the eggs of the human blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni directly within infected tissues of a living organism, rather than under artificial laboratory conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physics-based AI unlocks first global predictions of carbon cycling in ocean sediments
item.description: Researchers at The University of Manchester have developed a new physics-based artificial intelligence approach that, for the first time, enables accurate global-scale predictions of how dissolved organic carbon moves between seawater and marine sediments, a crucial but previously unquantifiable component of the planet's carbon cycle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Curved nanographene with five-, six- and seven-membered rings synthesized in two steps
item.description: Nanographenes can be considered molecular fragments of graphene, a 2D conductive material in which carbon atoms are connected in a honeycomb pattern. Because their electronic and photophysical properties vary depending on the size and shape of the molecule, nanographenes are expected to find applications in OLEDs, organic solar cells, organic field-effect transistors and more. Fuente: Phys.org.
